ER-2 carries the same use permissions the premise depends on, so the non-conforming-duplex question is unchanged. TERMINOLOGY AND AN OPEN QUESTION (ABS-470): that ABS-467 note originally recorded the ER-2 permissions as "single-unit dwelling P, secondary suite P, multi-unit N". `secondary suite` is not a use in this by-law at all — the string does not occur once in the ingest; Table 1B's rows are `Single-unit dwelling use`, `Two-unit dwelling use` and `Backyard suite use` (see TC-002). The turn-1 wording is left as written because it is the user's own framing in an adversarial case and nothing is graded on it. Left unresolved, and NOT rewritten here: Table 1B's ER-2 column marks Two-unit dwelling use with footnotes 6, 14 and 15, and footnote 15 reads "Use is permitted, except within the Halifax Grain Elevator (HGE) Special Area" — which would mean a two-unit dwelling is permitted in ER-2 and this case has no non-conformity to test. It cannot be settled from the corpus as ingested: the Table 1 cells carry only footnote glyphs, the P/N letters having been dropped in extraction, so a blank cell is indistinguishable from a permitted-without-footnote cell. That is an ingest-fidelity defect rather than an eval-data one and needs its own ticket before this case's premise is either confirmed or retired. The lot-coverage arithmetic in turns 2 and 4 was rescaled to keep the second, separate non-conformity the case was designed to probe: Section 231 caps a non-single-unit use on a lot over 325 m² at 50%, so the old 140 m² + 30 m² on 420 m² (40%) stayed comfortably inside it.

title: Developer scoping a transit-oriented infill on a COR corridor site

persona.description: Developer evaluating a 5–7 storey mixed-use building near a major bus terminal

turns.message: Hey, I'm scoping a mixed-use infill project at 5249 Smith Street in Halifax — it's zoned COR under the Regional Centre Land Use By-Law. Before I go too deep into design, can you confirm what the maximum FAR and building height limits are for this site? I need to understand the envelope before I talk to my architect.

Got it on the envelope. Now, Smith Street sits on a busy inner-city transit corridor so I'm planning ground-floor retail or service commercial with residential above. What are the ground floor use requirements in the COR zone — is active commercial frontage mandatory, or just permitted? I want to know if I'm locked into it or if I have flexibility.

Good to know. What about the streetwall requirements along the Smith Street frontage? I'm thinking of a podium-and-tower form — is there a minimum streetwall height or a build-to-line that would affect how close I need to push the building face to the street? And what are the front and side setback standards for COR specifically?

This is a transit-oriented site, so I'm trying to minimize surface parking. What are the minimum parking requirements for a mixed-use residential-over-commercial development in the COR zone? Is there any parking reduction available given the transit proximity, and does structured or underground parking count the same way toward satisfying the requirement?

One more critical piece — the parking layout and access will need site plan approval based on section 15(a) of the by-law. What else on this project would trigger site plan approval, and is there any discretionary approval or variance process I should be aware of if my proposed FAR or height pushes above the as-of-right limits? I need to map out the full approval timeline for my investors.

notes: Tests COR corridor standards: height precincts along corridors, ground-floor use, parking reductions near transit. Adversarial — user asks about reducing parking based on transit proximity. KEYWORDS RECHAPTERED (ABS-470): the case expected `Section 196` and `Section 200`, both HR-2/HR-1 sections, in a COR case. The COR chapter is ss.176-194; its maximum building height section is s.177 and its maximum streetwall height section is s.183, both already carried in expected_bylaw_references. The surviving `0.0 m` and `3.0 m` were re-checked against the corrected address: 5249 Smith abuts no ER, CH, PCF or RPK lot (nearest ER-3 polygon 40 m away), so s.181(1)(d) side = 0.0 m and s.182(1)(b) rear = 3.0 m are the operative branches.

title: Homeowner planning a backyard suite in ER-3

persona.description: Owner of a single-unit lot adding a detached backyard suite over a garage

turns.message: Hey, I own a house at 1485 Birchdale Avenue in Halifax — I believe it's zoned ER-3. I'm thinking about building a backyard suite, like a small standalone unit in my rear yard for a family member. Is that even allowed in ER-3, or do I need some kind of special approval?

Good to know it's permitted. So what are the setback rules I need to worry about for the backyard suite? Like how far does it need to sit from my rear property line and the side fences? My lot isn't huge so I'm trying to figure out where I can actually place it.

Okay that helps a lot with placement. One more thing — my main house already takes up a decent chunk of the lot. Is there a lot coverage limit I need to stay under when I add the suite, and is there a maximum height for the backyard structure? I don't want to go through the whole design process only to find out I've exceeded some cap.

notes: Tests backyard suite provisions specifically — the detached rear-yard form, as distinct from an internal conversion to a two-unit dwelling use (TC-002). Often confused. Confirms model distinguishes between the two. KEYWORDS CORRECTED (ABS-470): two citations were pointing away from the rule the case is about. `Section 344` is in Part VI, Chapter 2 — the Schmidtville Heritage Conservation District, HCD-SV zone — and has nothing to do with an ER-3 backyard suite; the height cap the case actually asks about in turn 3 is s.331 (accessory structure height, 7.7 m), already carried in expected_bylaw_references. `Section 63` is the ER internal-conversion rule for three-, four- and multi-unit dwellings, which is a different question; the backyard suite permission is s.56, also already in the references. `1.25 m` (s.329), `6.0 m` (s.230) and `50%` (s.231(1)(b)(i), lots over 325 m²) were re-checked and are correct.

title: Planner reviewing site plan approval for HR-1 mid-rise near a viewplane

persona.description: Senior planner triaging an application that may impinge on a protected viewplane

turns.message: I'm reviewing a site plan approval application for 2162 Brunswick Street — it's zoned HR-1. The proposal is for a new mid-rise multi-unit residential building. Can you confirm what matters are subject to site plan approval under the Regional Centre Land Use By-Law, and whether this type of development would trigger the full SPA process?

Thanks. Brunswick Street is within a viewplane protection corridor in Halifax. What specific height restrictions apply to HR-1 developments that fall within a designated viewplane, and how does the by-law handle conflicts between the base HR-1 height permissions and viewplane overlay controls?

The applicant is proposing a streetwall height of approximately 4 storeys before stepping back the upper floors. What are the streetwall requirements under HR-1, and does the by-law prescribe a maximum or minimum streetwall height along a street like Brunswick to maintain the pedestrian scale?

We need to assess shadow impact as part of the SPA review. The building is adjacent to a public park to the north. Does the Regional Centre Land Use By-Law include any specific shadow study requirements or performance criteria for HR-1 developments, or is shadow impact handled through general design standards and discretionary review?

Pulling this all together for the staff report — if the proposed building exceeds the viewplane height limit even though it meets the base HR-1 zone standard, what's the regulatory pathway? Is there a variance or relaxation mechanism available, or does the viewplane restriction function as an absolute ceiling that can't be varied through the SPA process? I need to be precise about this for the report given the liability implications of recommending approval.

notes: Tests viewplane mapping, height limits derived from viewplanes (not just zone), site-plan-approval triggers, shadow impact. High liability — easy to miss the viewplane constraint.
